title: Making Thinking Visible: The Philosophy of Process-Based Assessment
author: Jonathan Boymal
summary: Boymal examines process-based assessment, such as checkpoint drafts, reflection logs, oral defences and portfolios, which educators have adopted as a response to LLMs. He argues that this pragmatic shift conceals a deeper philosophical stance about what knowledge and education are. Drawing on Dewey, Merleau-Ponty, Foucault, Bourdieu, Fricker, Bergson and Schon, he shows that it treats knowledge as process, thinking as embodied, and learning as emergent. He also warns of three risks: vulnerability needs communities of trust, visibility can slide into surveillance and rehearsed performance, and the format can reproduce inequities favouring students fluent in institutional codes. His conclusion is that done well, the approach commits us to an education that cultivates thoughtful, attentive people.
points: Making thinking visible reframes knowledge as unfolding process, so drafts are the substance of learning and not merely an integrity measure.
Disclosure of uncertainty exposes developing selves, so process assessment only deepens learning inside communities of trust.
The practice can become surveillance or a performance of metacognition crafted to satisfy a rubric.
Equity requires diversifying the evidence of thinking we value, since habitus makes some students more fluent at visibility.
If learning is emergent, assessment design must reveal and support that emergence.
quotes: If assessment focuses only on final outputs, it risks obscuring the messy, challenging, and often meaningful process of students grappling with ideas; the very work where deep learning takes place.
In this light, drafts and checkpoints are not merely steps to enhance academic integrity; they are the very substance of learning, allowing us to see knowledge as provisional, unfolding, and alive.

Students who reveal uncertainty are not just sharing ideas, they are exposing their developing selves. Consequently, making thinking visible can only deepen learning if it is held within communities of trust.
The challenge, therefore, is to distinguish genuine, exploratory thinking from a performance of “metacognition” crafted solely to satisfy a rubric.
Without careful design, process-based assessments can unintentionally reproduce these injustices, rewarding the already articulate and penalising those less fluent in institutional codes.
Instead of freezing knowledge in a final snapshot, it captures thinking as it evolves.
If you believe learning is emergent, then you must design assessments that reveal and support that emergence.
